title: The Seventeenth of Tammuz
hookLine: a fast for the breach of Jerusalem's walls, beginning the Three Weeks

cards: Yom Kippur and the ninth of Av, the two long Jewish fasts, begin at sunset. This one begins at dawn. While it's still dark, some people are up eating a quick breakfast and drinking all the water they can.
Then nothing, no food, no drink, until the stars come out. There's no special meal at the end, no well-known melody, no crowd, and plenty of people walk past the date without noticing.
But in the synagogue the Torah is read, extra prayers are said, and a season has started. The day remembers a wall.

teach.b: Tammuz is a summer month, and on its seventeenth day the Mishnah gathers five disasters. Moses broke the tablets, coming down to find the golden calf. The daily offering in the Temple stopped.
The walls of Jerusalem were breached. A man called Apostomus burned a Torah scroll; nobody is sure who he was. And an idol was set up in the sanctuary.
The walls bring a puzzle. The book of Jeremiah says the Babylonians broke in on the ninth of the month, not the seventeenth.
The Talmud answers that the seventeenth belongs to the second wall, when the Romans broke in centuries later. The Jerusalem Talmud offers another answer: in the chaos, people lost track of the date.
Either way, the fast keeps the breach. A city doesn't fall the day its walls are breached; it falls weeks later.
The breach is the day the danger gets inside, the first crack. So this fast opens a season. Three weeks later comes the ninth of Av, when both Temples are remembered as destroyed.

teach.h: THREE WEEKS IN THE NARROW PLACES.
teach.b: The weeks between are named from Lamentations: bein hametzarim, between the narrow places. The fast runs from dawn to nightfall, and like the other minor fasts it excuses anyone ill, pregnant or nursing.
Customs vary: some communities hold no weddings in these weeks or play less music, and some people don't cut their hair. And there's a promise attached.
The prophet Zechariah says the fast of the fourth month, this one, will one day become a time of joy and gladness. Even the mourning is kept with an eye on mending.

how: On the Seventeenth of Tammuz observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, with a special Torah reading and added prayers; it begins the Three Weeks, when some communities hold no weddings and limit music until Tisha B'Av.

games.q: you're a sage, and the book of Jeremiah says the walls fell on the ninth, but the fast is on the seventeenth. what do you say?
o: move the fast to the ninth.
the seventeenth is the second wall, the Romans' breach.
games.why: the Babylonian Talmud says the seventeenth belongs to the second Temple's walls; the Jerusalem Talmud adds that in the chaos the date was lost.

practice: Walk, in your mind, around the walls of your life: a friendship, your health, your work, the way you speak to someone close.
Look for one place where something small has started to give, a message you keep not answering, a resentment that's grown a little, and just name it, gently; noticing early is the work.
